product.title: Lao 101 - A1 (English Edition)
product.description: Twenty Assimil-style self-study units that take you from zero to A1 Lao: the toned pronunciation is printed right above every Lao word, with short dialogues, word-for-word translations that show how Lao builds its sentences, grammar notes, vocabulary, exercises, and an answer key. Also included: a table of all 27 consonants with their three classes, a map of the six Vientiane tones, a list of classifiers, a summary of particles, and a glossary. Written for English speakers — each unit targets one of the spots that actually trip learners up, from tones that change the meaning to the particles ເດີ້ and ເນາະ that decide whether you sound friendly or curt.

cover_design.label: LAO
cover_design.ringkas: A self-study course in Lao for complete beginners — from bargaining at Talat Sao to telling the story of a trip you've already taken.
cover_design.catatan: The toned pronunciation is printed above every word; a word-for-word translation sits under every line of dialogue.

blocks.text: Lao is a language few people choose to learn, and that's exactly your advantage. Native speakers almost never meet a foreigner who can speak Lao, so your first sentence — however short — is nearly always answered with a big smile and ten more sentences.

And the language is friendlier than it looks. The sentence *ຂ້ອຍກິນເຂົ້າ* is built word for word like English: "I — eat — rice." No verb conjugation, no plurals, no noun genders, no endings to memorize. If it happened yesterday, you simply add the word "yesterday."

Only two things look scary on the surface: the script, and the fact that written Lao flows **without spaces between words**. Neither is a wall; both are doors with stiff hinges for the first week. This course loosens those hinges with one simple decision: every Lao word, from the first page to the last, carries its pronunciation right above it.
The real difficulties of Lao lie in three places, and this course is built around all three.

**First, tones.** The same syllable can mean several different things depending on the rise and fall of your voice. *ຂາ khǎa* is leg; *ຄ້າ kháa* is to trade; *ຂ້າ khàa* is to kill. To an English-speaking ear this feels impossible in week one and perfectly normal by month two — as long as tones are practiced from the very first word, not postponed until "later, once I'm fluent." That's why **every word in this course is printed with its tone mark**, without exception.

**Second, classifiers.** "Two bottles of water" in Lao is *ນ້ຳສອງຂວດ* — "water two bottle." English already does this with some nouns (two **bottles** of water, three **head** of cattle, a **pair** of shoes); Lao simply does it with every noun you count. All you need is the list of classifiers and their slightly different word order.

**Third, politeness that isn't carried by any single word.** Lao has no gendered pair of particles like Thai *ครับ/ค่ะ*. Its politeness lives in **the choice of pronoun** (*ຂ້ອຍ* or *ຂ້ານ້ອຍ*), in the word *ເຈົ້າ*, which means both "yes" and "you," and in tail particles like *ເດີ້* and *ເນາະ* that soften a sentence. A grammatically perfect sentence can sound curt without its tail — and that's not a grammar mistake but a mistake in attitude.

A note for anyone who has studied Thai: you're holding a big shortcut. A large share of the core vocabulary overlaps, and the two scripts are close siblings. But don't treat Lao as the same language with a different accent — the spelling differs, the tones differ, and some words that sound alike have shifted in meaning. This course marks those spots with ⚠️.
The explanations are deliberately short. What's long isn't the theory but the practice.

blocks.title: Before you start
items: Set aside 20–30 uninterrupted minutes, not two hours chopped into pieces. Languages stick through short, frequent repetition, not one long assault.

Read aloud — in Lao this isn't a suggestion but a requirement. Tones can't be learned with your eyes. If you read *ຂາ* silently, your brain reads it with no tone at all, and the wrong version is the one that sticks.

The six tones are practiced from the first word, not in a special chapter. Every time you see a mark like ˊ ˋ ˆ ˇ ˉ in the pronunciation, voice its rise and fall. Ten seconds per word, and tones stop being theory.

Don't wait for perfect tones before you dare to speak. Lao people are used to guessing from context: point at a glass and say *ນ້ຳ* in any tone, and water still arrives. What isn't forgiven is a blank face without a smile — in Laos that's felt far more than a missed tone.

blocks.text: Enjoy the journey. *ໂຊກດີເດີ້! Sôok-dii dòe!*

front.title: Contents
front.intro: This course works best in order — each unit reuses what the previous ones set up.

blocks.text: This course is designed for **self-study**. Each unit is meant to be finished in one sitting, about 20–30 minutes. What matters isn't how fast you move forward but how often you come back.
Every unit has the same structure, and the order is deliberate:

items: **Dialogue** — first read the Lao aloud, following the pronunciation above each word. Don't look at the English on the first try. Let your ears work before your brain demands an explanation.

**Literal translation** — the small italic line under the meaning. It's the part people skip most, yet it's where you see how Lao *thinks*. Example: *ໄປໃສມາ* literally means "go where come?", not "where have you been?".
**Notes** — short explanations of whatever felt strange.
**Vocabulary** — the unit's new words, with toned pronunciation.
**Exercises** — do them without looking at the key. Mistakes are part of the process.
**Answer key** — open it only after you've really tried.

blocks.title: Wave review
items: From Unit 3 on, each unit asks you to review an earlier unit — usually two steps back, the right distance to make your memory work without feeling like starting from scratch. Do it in reverse: cover the Lao, look at the English, and rebuild the Lao sentences from memory — **tones included**.
This is what turns "I understood it once" into "I can use it." Don't skip it.

blocks.title: One habit special to this course
items: Whenever you meet a new word, say it **three times in a row with the same tone**. Lao tones live in your muscles, not your memory; a word read only once will come out with a random tone the moment you get nervous.

If you're unsure of a word's tone, don't guess from its meaning — check the mark in the pronunciation. This course prints it at every appearance of a word, not just the first, precisely so you never have a reason to guess.

blocks.text: One last rule: **say it out loud**. Lao rewards that more than anything, because half of it simply isn't on paper.

front.title: The pronunciation system used in this course

blocks.text: The **pronunciation** shown throughout this course uses a romanization common in English-language textbooks for Lao and Thai. Most letters sound roughly as you'd expect; the vowels have their "continental" values (as in Spanish or Italian), not English ones. There are just four things to learn below.
1. Tone marks above the vowel

head: Mark
Tone

rows: flat, but clearly lower than your normal pitch

blocks.text: Six marks — one more than Thai, which has five. Don't panic: in everyday conversation, only **three** cause most misunderstandings — rising, falling, and low. The rest settle in on their own after a few units.
The mark always sits on the **main vowel** of the syllable. If a word has two syllables, each carries its own mark: *ສະບາຍດີ* → *sa-baai-dii*.
2. Long vowels are written double

Vowel length in Lao **changes the meaning**, just as seriously as tone does — the script even uses different letters for the two. So long vowels are always written double: *aa, ii, uu, ee, oo*. If you see a single letter, keep it short.

*ສະ-ບາຍ-ດີ* is written *sa-baai-dii* so you know there are three beats, not one. The hyphen doesn't mean a pause — say it smoothly.

front.title: The Lao script: how it works, in two pages

blocks.text: You **don't need** to master this chapter before Unit 1. The pronunciation is printed above every word throughout the course, so you can keep moving while the script slowly sinks in. Read this chapter once now, then come back whenever something puzzles you.

The Lao script is a close relative of the Thai script — both descend from old Khmer script, which descends from South Indian scripts. The difference is that Lao was **streamlined** in the 20th century: letters with the same sound were merged, the number of letters was cut, and spelling was made to follow pronunciation. As a result, Lao script is easier than Thai — 27 consonants versus 44, and almost no letters that exist "only for loanwords."
There are four things you need to know about how it works.
1. Every consonant carries a vowel, and the vowel can go anywhere

Vowel signs can appear **to the right, to the left, above, below**, or surround the consonant on two sides at once. What confuses beginners most: some vowels are written **before** their consonant but pronounced **after** it.
So when you see ເ or ແ or ໂ or ໄ, don't read it yet — find the consonant to its right, read that consonant, then attach the vowel.
2. No spaces between words — spaces separate SENTENCES

This is the biggest surprise for English readers. *ຂ້ອຍຢູ່ວຽງຈັນ* is one unbroken string, and it means "I live in Vientiane." Spaces only appear at the boundaries of long phrases or sentences. The good news: the human brain learns to cut these strings much faster than you'd think, because Lao words are short and their syllable patterns repeat.

In this course every word is already cut for you by the pronunciation above it. After Unit 8 or 9, try covering the pronunciation line now and then and cutting the words yourself — you'll be surprised.
3. Three consonant classes decide the tone

This is the heart of the Lao writing system, and the reason the "Six tones" chapter comes next. Every consonant belongs to one of three classes — **high**, **middle**, **low**. The tone of a syllable is worked out from three things at once: the class of its first consonant, whether there's a tone mark, and how the syllable ends.

You **don't need** to work it out now. This course prints the tone for you at every appearance of a word. Just remember one fact: two letters that sound exactly alike — *ຂ* and *ຄ* are both *kh* — exist precisely to **distinguish tones**, not sounds.
4. The letter ຫ is used as a tone raiser

*ຫ* on its own sounds like *h*. But when it stands **in front of** a low-class consonant such as ງ ຍ ນ ມ ລ ວ, it isn't pronounced — its job is to move that consonant into the high class, which changes the tone. Some of these pairs have even merged into a single letter: **ໜ** = ຫ+ນ, **ໝ** = ຫ+ມ, **ຫຼ** = ຫ+ລ.

blocks.title: If you've studied the Thai script
items: The letter shapes are related and mostly easy to guess, but **don't guess the spelling**. Lao spells words by sound; Thai spells them by their Pali/Sanskrit origin. The same word can be written with completely different letters.
The letter ຣ (*r*) is hardly used in modern Laos — its sound has merged into ລ (*l*). Names written with *r* in Thailand are written and pronounced with *l* in Laos.
Lao has an *ny-* sound at the start of words (ຍ, ຫຍ) with no written equivalent in modern Thai.

blocks.text: Twenty-seven consonants, grouped by **tone class**. The "name" column is how Lao people call the letter when spelling — just like "bee" for B — and it's almost always "sound + example word."
MIDDLE-class consonants (8 letters)

The letter **ອ** is the strangest and most important: it's an "empty" consonant. Because every Lao vowel must attach to a consonant, words that start with a vowel use ອ as a prop. *ອາຫານ aa-hǎan* (food) is really "ອ + າ."
HIGH-class consonants (8 letters)
LOW-class consonants (11 letters)

Notice the pairs that sound the same but belong to different classes: ຂ/ຄ, ສ/ຊ, ຖ/ທ, ຜ/ພ, ຝ/ຟ, ຫ/ຮ. These six pairs are Lao's main tool for writing tones. The letter ຣ (*r*) is still on the official list but practically unused.
The most common vowels
Lao numerals

Lao numerals are still used on official documents, house numbers, and some price lists in traditional markets. In the city, Western digits are far more common — but step into a government office and ໑໒໓ show up again.

front.title: Six tones: the one thing that changes everything

blocks.text: Vientiane Lao has **six** tones. That number sounds frightening until you realize that English also uses rising and falling pitch all the time — just for a different job. English uses it for **sentences** ("He's going." versus "He's going?"). Lao uses it for **words**.

That means one practical thing: when you ask a question in Lao, don't raise your voice at the end the way English does. Questions are marked by **words**, not by pitch — and raising your voice at the end actually turns your last word into a different word.

blocks.text: Practice methods that actually work

items: **Use your hand.** Move your palm along with the tone as you say it. It sounds silly and it works: tones are stored as movement, not as knowledge.

**Practice in pairs, not one at a time.** Say *ຂາ khǎa* and *ຂ້າ khàa* back to back until you hear the difference yourself. A tone practiced alone sounds right in your head and wrong to everyone else.
**Record yourself.** Once a week is enough. Compare with native audio. A gap you can't hear while speaking jumps out on playback.
**Never say a word without its tone "just for now."** A word that first goes in without a tone sticks that way, and fixing it costs far more than learning it right from the start.

blocks.title: Good news about tones
items: In a full sentence, a missed tone **rarely** stops people from understanding — context and the surrounding words cover for it. The real danger is a word standing alone: a one-word answer, a one-word command, a name.

Lao people are used to hearing many accents — northern Lao, southern Lao, Isan from across the Mekong — so their ears are flexible. What they're not used to hearing is a sentence with **no tones at all**, because it sounds like a robot.
After about 300 words your tones start to run on their own: you stop calculating and start feeling "this word sounds like this." This course contains about 700 words.

blocks.text: Enough theory. Open Unit 1.
The order is always **noun + number + classifier**: *ເບຍສອງແກ້ວ bia sǎwng kêeo* = "beer two glass." For "one," the number often moves to the end: *ເບຍແກ້ວໜຶ່ງ* sounds more natural than *ເບຍໜຶ່ງແກ້ວ*.

blocks.title: A shortcut if you forget
items: For any object whose classifier you don't know, use **ອັນ *an***. People will understand and won't find it rude — much like a learner of English saying "thing" for everything.
For people, **ຄົນ *khón*** is always safe except in formal situations.
If you're pointing at the thing, the classifier can stand alone without the noun: *ເອົາອັນນີ້ ao an nîi* = "I'll take this one."

blocks.text: ⚠️ If you're coming from Thai: Lao does **not** put *ครับ/ค่ะ* at the end of every sentence. Doing so instantly makes you sound like a Thai person speaking Lao. The closest equivalents in feeling are *ເດີ້* and *ເນາະ* — and neither goes in every sentence, only now and then.
Numbers

Two traps: **11 is not** *síp-nʉ̀ng* but *síp-ét*, and that *-ét* pattern applies to every 1 in the ones place (21, 31, 101). And **20 is not** *sǎwng-síp* but *saao* — a separate word you have to memorize.

Lao money is the **ກີບ *kìip***. Because it's worth little, the numbers you hear at the market are almost always in the tens of thousands: *ຊາວຫ້າພັນ saao-hāa-phán* = 25,000. In fast speech, *ພັນ* is often dropped: people say "25" and both sides know it means 25,000.

blocks.text: Days, months, and time words

The Lao month names are long and rarely used in speech; people usually say **"month number…"**: *ເດືອນໜຶ່ງ dʉan nʉ̀ng* (January), *ເດືອນສິບສອງ dʉan síp-sǎwng* (December). That's the safe option, and it's always understood.

blocks.text: Notice that *ເຈົ້າ jâo* does two jobs at once: "you" and "yes." Only position tells them apart — at the start or in the middle of a sentence it means "you"; standing alone as an answer it means "yes."
Question words

The big rule that sets Lao apart from English: **question words don't move to the front**. They stand exactly where the answer will stand. *ເຈົ້າກິນຫຍັງ* = "you eat what?" — the same order as the answer "I eat rice."

⚠️ *ໃກ້ kâi* (near) and *ໄກ kai* (far) differ **only in tone and length**. This is the pair most likely to get beginners literally lost. Practice them back to back until you hear the difference yourself.

If you've reached this page after working through all twenty units, you now have about 700 words and the whole A1 grammar framework: asking, bargaining, ordering, telling what happened, planning what's ahead, and asking for help. That's enough for everyday life in Vientiane without English.
What comes next isn't "new material" but **flight hours**. Three suggestions, in order of payoff.

items: **Listen without understanding.** Play Lao radio or a news channel in the background while you do other things. The goal isn't to understand but to tune your ear to the rhythm. After a few weeks, words start popping out of the stream of sound on their own.

**Read signs.** It's the best script practice there is, and it's free. Shop signs, street signs, menus on the wall — all short, repetitive, and with pictures as clues. After this course you can already read most of them.
**Find one person to talk to, not ten.** One regular conversation partner you meet often gives far better results than ten short chats with different people, because you build a shared vocabulary.

blocks.title: If you want to move on to A2
items: Expand your verb helpers: *ຄົງ khóng* (probably), *ອາດ àat* (perhaps), *ເລີຍ lóei* (so, right away), *ພໍ phaw* (as soon as…, enough).
Move into complex sentences with *ທີ່ thìi* (that, which), *ຖ້າ thàa* (if), *ເພາະວ່າ phaw vàa* (because), *ເຖິງແມ່ນວ່າ thǒeng mèen vàa* (although).
Learn the formal written language — letters, announcements, and the news use Pali-Sanskrit vocabulary that differs from conversation. It's a leap of its own, best taken once your conversation flows.

blocks.text: One last thing. Lao speakers rarely hear foreigners making the effort. Every time you use it — even just *ຂອບໃຈເດີ້* at a food stall — you give something money can't buy. Use it.
*ໂຊກດີເດີ້! Sôok-dii dòe!*
